title: Synthetic negative corpus generator
description:
Generate controlled negative test files (files that should NOT trigger detection) with seeded randomness. Tests precision — do we avoid non-secrets?

## Research basis
- TruffleHog DefaultFalsePositives: "example", "xxxxxx", "aaaaaa", "abcde", "00000", "sample", "*****". Aho-Corasick wordlist filtering with fp_words.txt, fp_badlist.txt, fp_programmingbooks.txt, fp_uuids.txt. [P1.5.F4, evidence 3]
- secrets-patterns-db: 1600+ regex patterns. No negative test cases published. [P1.4, evidence 2]
- Nosey Parker: Rule schema requires negative_examples — strongest enforcement model. [P1.5.F5, evidence 3]
- CredData: 73,842 labeled lines, only 6% True. 94% of labeled data is negative — shows realistic ratio. [P1.3.F3]

## Negative categories to generate

Each category targets specific scanner gates (see src/api.rs:560-755):

1. **Entropy decoys** (targets: entropy gate in src/engine/helpers/entropy.rs)
   - Random base62 strings at lengths 20, 32, 40, 64
   - Random base64 strings at lengths 24, 44, 88
   - High-entropy but non-secret: compressed data fragments

2. **Hash look-alikes** (targets: regex patterns, offline_validation)
   - SHA1 (40 hex), SHA256 (64 hex), UUIDv4, MongoDB ObjectIDs, Git SHAs, Snowflake IDs

3. **Format perturbations** (targets: offline_validation in src/api.rs:873-896)
   - AKIA prefix + wrong length, ghp_ prefix + wrong charset, sk_live_ + invalid checksum

4. **Context traps** (targets: value_suppressors_any, keywords_any)
   - High-entropy strings near "example", "test", "dummy", "PLACEHOLDER"
   - Strings in comments, disabled code, near localhost

5. **JWT headers** (targets: JWT rule regex)
   - Valid structure with garbage payload, three dot-separated base64 segments

6. **Unicode/homoglyph** (targets: char_class ASCII gate)
   - Cyrillic lookalikes, non-ASCII at secret-like positions

## Output format
- Directory of files with .synth-neg.ndjson ground truth
- Each truth entry: {"path":"...","start":N,"end":M,"label":"neg","category":"entropy_decoy"}
- Seeded RNG (default seed=42) for deterministic generation

## Implementation sketch

    pub struct SynthConfig { pub seed: u64, pub files_per_category: usize, pub output_dir: PathBuf }
    pub fn generate_all(config: &SynthConfig) -> Vec<GeneratedFile>
    // One fn per category, all take &mut SmallRng for determinism

## Scanner gates to stress-test (from src/api.rs)
- entropy: EntropySpec (Shannon bpb threshold + optional min-entropy)
- keywords_any: presence of domain keywords near candidate
- char_class: CharClassSpec (lowercase ASCII percentage gate)
- local_context: LocalContextSpec (assignment shape, quoting)
- offline_validation: CRC32Base62, GithubFinegrainedPat, AwsAccessKey, etc.
- value_suppressors_any: "EXAMPLE", "PLACEHOLDER", etc.
- must_contain: cheap substring pre-check

## Acceptance criteria
1. cargo run --bin make-synth-neg -- --seed 42 --out /tmp/synth generates files
2. Running scanner against output: zero findings (all negatives correctly rejected)
3. Same seed -> bit-for-bit identical output
4. Ground truth NDJSON loads into eval harness via synthetic corpus loader

title: Add per-item byte limit to connector streaming paths
description:
## Context
Code review of PR #160 (connector pipeline item-level read/scan). Security review finding.

## Current State
Both `stream_item_via_open()` and `stream_item_via_range_read()` in `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs` have no upper bound on total bytes read per item. A misbehaving connector could stream bytes indefinitely (returning small non-zero reads that never reach EOF), causing unbounded CPU consumption and preventing page checkpoint advancement.

## Desired State
Add a configurable `max_item_bytes: u64` field to `ConnectorConfig` with a sensible default (e.g., 256 MB). Both streaming paths should track total bytes read and return `ReadError::permanent()` when the limit is exceeded.

## Implementation Guidance
- Add `max_item_bytes: u64` to `ConnectorConfig` (with default 256 * 1024 * 1024)
- Track cumulative bytes in the streaming loop (`offset` already does this)
- After each read: if `offset > cfg.max_item_bytes`, return `ReadError::permanent("item exceeded max byte limit")`
- Add validation in `ConnectorConfig::validate()`

## Code References
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:401-445` — `stream_item_via_open`
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:453-504` — `stream_item_via_range_read`
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:94-107` — `ConnectorConfig` struct

## Related Work
None found — this is a new defensive guard.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `ConnectorConfig` has a `max_item_bytes` field with sensible default
- [ ] Both streaming paths enforce the limit
- [ ] Test covering limit enforcement
- [ ] `cargo test -p scanner-rs --lib` passes
- [ ] `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` clean
close_reason: Added max_item_bytes field to ConnectorConfig (default 256 MiB), validation in validate(), enforcement in stream_chunks with permanent ReadError on breach

title: Zero-cost shared-core migration: scanner-rs engine into gossip-rs harness
description:

- gossip-rs scan loop owns lease/checkpoint/park/complete and explicitly does not do detection fan-out.
- gossip-connectors has a production filesystem connector implementation.
- scanner-rs connector pipeline exists but currently processes page items synchronously and is not yet proven as a zero-regression replacement.

## Desired State
Deliver a phased, zero-cost shared-core migration where:
1. standalone scanner-rs remains first-class and unchanged by default;

title: Add hand-rolled logistic regression post-filter classifier
description:
## Overview

Implement a hand-rolled logistic regression classifier with 10-15 features, pre-trained offline in Python and embedded as Rust const arrays. No ML framework dependency. Contributes to confidence score as post-filter.

## Motivation

Multiple weak signals combined outperform any single threshold. CredSweeper (Samsung) uses ONNX neural network with 18 features. Hand-rolled LR avoids framework overhead.

**Evidence**: Level 2-3. CredSweeper (Samsung, open-source). 3 agents recommended hand-rolled. All ML frameworks (linfa, smartcore, tract) are overkill for 10-15 feature inference.

## Feature vector (all computable in <1us)

| # | Feature | Source | Cost |
|---|---------|--------|------|
| 1 | Shannon entropy | Already computed | 0ns |
| 2 | Chi-squared | Task 1 histogram | ~100ns |
| 3 | Min-entropy | Task 1 histogram | ~50ns |
| 4 | Length | len() | ~0ns |
| 5 | Uppercase ratio | Task 6 or scalar | ~10ns |
| 6 | Lowercase ratio | Task 6 or scalar | ~10ns |
| 7 | Digit ratio | Task 6 or scalar | ~10ns |
| 8 | Special char ratio | Task 6 or scalar | ~10ns |
| 9 | Max consecutive same-class run | Single pass | ~50ns |
| 10 | Has repeated trigram | Hash-based check | ~100ns |
| 11 | Serial correlation | Task 2 | ~100ns |
| 12 | Unique bytes / total | From histogram | ~50ns |

### Inference

```rust
const WEIGHTS: [f32; 12] = [ /* trained offline */ ];
const BIAS: f32 = /* trained offline */;

fn classify_secret(features: &[f32; 12]) -> f32 {
    let dot: f32 = features.iter().zip(WEIGHTS.iter()).map(|(f, w)| f * w).sum();
    dot + BIAS // raw logit; sigmoid > 0.5 iff logit > 0
}
```

Cost: ~5-20ns for 12-feature dot product. No allocation.

### Confidence integration
- logit > 2.0: confidence += 3
- logit > 0.5: confidence += 1
- logit < -0.5: confidence -= 1
- logit < -2.0: confidence -= 3

## Training workflow (offline, Python)

1. Collect labeled dataset from scanner-rs output (TP/FP)
2. Extract feature vectors
3. Train: scikit-learn LogisticRegression(C=1.0)
4. Evaluate: precision/recall/F1 on test set
5. Export: weights + bias as Rust const arrays
6. Validate: Rust inference matches Python predictions

### Files to modify

1. **New file: src/engine/ml_filter.rs**: Feature extraction + LR inference + confidence
2. **src/engine/window_validate.rs**: Call classifier, contribute to confidence
3. **src/engine/scratch.rs**: Feature vector scratch space
4. **scripts/**: Python training script

### Dependencies
- Task 1 (chi-squared, min-entropy features)
- Task 6 (SIMD char-class ratios)
- Task 9 (confidence scoring model)

### Risk analysis
- Overfitting: Simple LR with 12 features is low risk
- Dataset bias: Need diverse repos for training
- Magic numbers: Document training process, keep script in repo
- Graceful degradation: logit near 0 contributes 0 to confidence

### References
- CredSweeper: https://github.com/Samsung/CredSweeper
- scikit-learn LogisticRegression

title: Cross-Rule Dedup: Best Interpretation Wins
description:
## Objective
Reduce duplicate findings where multiple rules match the same logical occurrence, keeping the most useful interpretation (best-confidence winner) while preserving deterministic behavior.

## Why this epic exists
Without cross-rule dedup, the pipeline can emit multiple findings for one occurrence (for example generic entropy + specific credential rule), inflating false positives and distorting measurement.

## Design contract
Winner policy within a dedupe group:
- highest `confidence_score` wins
- ties break by lexicographically smallest rule name
- final deterministic tie-break by stable rule id/order

Grouping identity by layer:
- Eval-harness (existing): `(path, byte_start, byte_end)`
- Scanner runtime (required): rule-agnostic location + hash identity with **conditional span participation**:
  - base: `root_hint_start`, `root_hint_end`, `norm_hash`
  - include `span_start`/`span_end` when `dedupe_with_span == true`

This split reflects available runtime data and existing engine/store semantics; both layers must produce deterministic winner selection.

## Scope
This epic covers both implementation and measurement:
1. Eval-harness implementation and controls (completed)
2. Scanner runtime implementation with backend parity (blocking + uring)
3. Confidence metadata integrity checks for fair winner selection
4. Deterministic synthetic overlap corpus for controlled evaluation
5. 2x2 measurement matrix to choose production defaults

title: Rule ablation testing for noise identification
description:
Run eval with each rule disabled in turn. Report the AP/F1 delta per rule removal. Identifies: (a) rules that contribute most to recall, (b) rules that contribute most noise (AP increases when removed).

## Research basis
- With 223 rules in default_rules.yaml, some are inevitably noisy.
- detect-secrets audit --stats quantifies per-plugin signal-to-noise ratio, but requires manual labeling. Ablation is automatic. [P1.5.F6]
- No open-source scanner publishes per-rule accuracy metrics. [P1.5.F8]

## Algorithm
1. Run full eval (all rules) -> baseline metrics
2. For each rule R in 1..223:
   a. Run scanner with rule R disabled
   b. Compute metrics on same corpus
   c. Record delta: AP_baseline - AP_without_R, F1 delta
3. Sort rules by: (a) recall contribution (AP drops most), (b) noise contribution (AP increases most)
4. Output: sorted table of rule ablation impact

## Implementation sketch
- Requires live-scan mode (not pre-computed findings)
- Parallelize: N+1 independent scans, embarrassingly parallel
- Use rayon or spawn scanner processes with --exclude-rule flag
- Emit CSV: rule_name, ap_with, ap_without, ap_delta, f1_delta

## CLI
    eval-harness ablation --corpus <dir> --format csv|json|table

## Acceptance criteria
1. Ablation of a known-noisy rule shows AP increase
2. Ablation of a known-good rule shows AP decrease
3. N+1 evaluations complete (parallelized, not serial)
4. Output sorted by absolute AP delta descending

title: Add file-path-based skip lists for known-benign file types
description:
## Overview

Add configurable file-path-based skip lists that prevent scanning of known-benign file types (binary files, lock files, vendor directories, build artifacts). Operates at scheduler level before content is read, providing the cheapest possible FP reduction.

## Motivation

Lock files (package-lock.json, yarn.lock), binary files (.exe, .dll, .png), and vendor directories contain hash-like strings and encoded data that trigger false positives. Skipping them avoids all downstream processing.

**Evidence**: Level 3. Gitleaks gitleaks.toml has extensive path exclusions. detect-secrets excludes 40+ extensions. GitHub AI detection skips SVG, PNG, JPEG, CSV, TXT, SQL. 3 agents identified.

## Skip list categories

### Binary/media (never contain secrets)
Extensions: .bmp, .gif, .ico, .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .svg, .webp, .mp3, .mp4, .wav, .eot, .ttf, .woff, .woff2, .pdf, .zip, .tar, .gz, .bz2, .xz, .7z, .jar

### Compiled artifacts
Extensions: .exe, .dll, .so, .dylib, .o, .obj, .a, .lib, .class, .pyc, .wasm

### Lock files (contain hashes that look like secrets)
Filenames: package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, Gemfile.lock, Cargo.lock, poetry.lock, composer.lock, go.sum, mix.lock, Pipfile.lock

### Dependency/vendor directories
Paths: node_modules/, vendor/, .bundle/, __pycache__/, dist/, build/, target/, .git/

### Build tool wrappers
Filenames: gradlew, gradlew.bat, mvnw, mvnw.cmd

## Implementation

### Configuration

```rust
pub struct PathSkipSpec {
    pub skip_extensions: Vec<String>,
    pub skip_filenames: Vec<String>,
    pub skip_directories: Vec<String>,
}
```

### Integration point
Operates at scheduler/chunk level, NOT in window_validate.rs:
- Before file content is read/scanned, check path against skip lists
- If matched, skip entire file (saves all downstream processing)

### Files to modify

1. **src/api.rs**: Add PathSkipSpec struct with defaults
2. **Scheduler-level**: Path check before content scanning
3. **default_rules.yaml**: Global skip list configuration
4. **src/rules/yaml.rs**: Parse skip list from YAML

### Design
- Ship sensible defaults (all categories above)
- Allow user override: add/remove skips
- Per-rule overrides for special cases

### Risk analysis
- False negatives: Secrets CAN exist in lock files (credentials in package URLs). Low risk but non-zero.
- Mitigation: Make configurable. Document the recall/precision tradeoff.
- Cost: String comparison on file metadata, effectively zero
- Battle-tested: Gitleaks uses these defaults across millions of repos

### References
- Gitleaks config/gitleaks.toml
- detect-secrets core/scan.py: binary extension exclusions
- GitHub AI detection docs: file type exclusions
close_reason: File-path-based skip functionality implemented

title: Add .env structured parsing as ExtractableFormat
description:
## Context

.env files are the highest-density secret source in real-world repositories. They contain KEY=VALUE lines where values often hold API keys, database passwords, and tokens. Currently scanner-rs scans .env files as plain text, but structured parsing extracts clean key-value pairs without comment noise, improving both precision (reduced FPs) and recall (proper handling of quoted multi-line values).

Evidence: Phase 4 contrarian searcher identified this as the strongest alternative missed by initial synthesis. .env files are already scanned as text but structural extraction is additive — provides focused values alongside existing full-text scanning.

## Current State

- .env files are scanned as ContentVerdict::Text (src/content_policy/mod.rs:79-91)
- ExtractableFormat enum at src/content_policy/mod.rs:40-49 has 4 variants: Ipynb, JavaClass, JarWar, Pyc
- match_extractable_extension at src/content_policy/mod.rs:101-116 maps extensions to formats
- extract_content dispatcher at src/content_policy/extract.rs:73-85 routes to extractors
- Extractor trait at src/content_policy/extract.rs:23-42
- .env is NOT in SKIP_EXTS (path policy), so it does get opened and read
- path_policy benchmarks already include b".env" (benches/path_policy.rs:38)

## Desired State

- New ExtractableFormat::DotEnv variant
- New src/content_policy/dotenv.rs module with DotEnvExtractor implementing Extractor
- classify_content returns BinaryExtractable(DotEnv) for .env paths
- Extractor parses KEY=VALUE lines: strips comments (#), handles quoted values ("...", single-quotes), handles export prefix
- Outputs KEY=VALUE lines (not just values) to preserve keyword context for rules anchoring on key names
- Zero allocation beyond the provided out buffer

## Implementation Guidance

### Files to modify:
1. `src/content_policy/mod.rs` — Add DotEnv to ExtractableFormat enum, add dotfile basename matching (file_extension returns None for .env, need special-case check for filenames starting with .env)
2. `src/content_policy/dotenv.rs` (new) — DotEnvExtractor struct implementing Extractor trait
3. `src/content_policy/extract.rs` — Add dispatch arm for DotEnv
4. `src/content_policy/mod.rs` — Add pub mod dotenv declaration

### Parse logic:
- Iterate lines (split on \n, handle \r\n)
- Skip empty lines and lines starting with # (after trimming whitespace)
- For KEY=VALUE lines: find first =, extract full line (keeping KEY= prefix for rule anchoring)
- Handle double-quoted values: strip surrounding quotes, process \n, \t, \\, \" escapes
- Handle single-quoted values: strip surrounding quotes (no escape processing per dotenv spec)
- Handle unquoted values: trim trailing whitespace
- Handle export KEY=VALUE prefix (strip export keyword)
- Respect EXTRACT_OUTPUT_CAP from extract module

### Key design decision:
Output KEY=VALUE lines, not just values. This preserves keyword context for rules that anchor on key names like password=, api_key=, etc. The existing base64/URL transforms strip context; the .env extractor should NOT do this.

## Code References

```rust
// src/content_policy/mod.rs:40-49 — ExtractableFormat enum
// src/content_policy/mod.rs:101-116 — match_extractable_extension
// src/content_policy/extract.rs:23-42 — Extractor trait
// src/content_policy/extract.rs:73-85 — extract_content dispatcher
// src/content_policy/ipynb.rs — Template for a simple extractor implementation
```

- Malformed lines (no =) are skipped gracefully (no panic)
- Unit tests cover all parse edge cases

description:
Task 11: Write comprehensive eval harness documentation

Priority: P1 | Type: task | Depends on: Task 10 (scratch-8mnx)

Why: The eval harness is a critical tool for measuring and maintaining scanner accuracy. Without thorough documentation, contributors won't know how to run evals, interpret results, or integrate them into their workflow. This task produces a standalone guide that makes the harness self-service.

What to Document:

1. What it is: Overview of the eval harness — its purpose, architecture, and the modules involved (corpus loaders, finding parser, matcher, metrics engine, regression checker, reporter).

2. Why it exists: Motivation — measuring scanner precision/recall against labeled ground-truth corpora, catching accuracy regressions before release, benchmarking new rules against known datasets (CredData, LeakyRepo, synthetic).

3. How it works (internals): Corpus loaders (CredData CSV parser, LeakyRepo CSV parser, synthetic JSON manifest loader), Finding parser (JSONL normalization from scanner output), Matching logic (how findings are matched to ground-truth labels by byte offset, line number, rule ID), Metrics computation (PRC-AUC calculation, precision/recall curves), Regression verdicts (baseline comparison, pass/warn/block thresholds).

4. How to use it (CLI guide): All three corpus types (creddata, leaky-repo, synthetic), both input modes (pre-existing JSONL findings file vs live --scan-corpus mode), output formats (--format json, --format table), baseline comparison (--baseline prev.json workflow), exit codes (0=Pass/Warn, 1=Block, 2=argument/runtime error).

5. When to use it: After modifying detection rules, before releases to verify no accuracy regressions, in CI pipelines for automated regression gating, when adding new secret types to measure coverage, when tuning confidence scoring or post-filters.

6. Interpreting results: Reading PRC-AUC scores and what good/bad values look like, precision vs recall trade-offs for secret detection, understanding regression verdicts (pass/warn/block) and thresholds, debugging false positives and false negatives using harness output.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Documentation covers all six sections above
- Includes concrete CLI examples with expected output
- Includes a quick-start section for first-time users
- Reviewed for accuracy against the implemented code

title: Add xz/LZMA decompression support (.tar.xz, .xz, .txz)
description:
## Context

.tar.xz / .txz / .xz archives are the standard distribution format for GNU/Linux source tarballs (coreutils, glibc, gcc, kernel). The lzma-rs crate is pure Rust with #![forbid(unsafe_code)], providing streaming decompression via features=["stream"] since v0.2.0. The streaming API is Write-based (push model) and needs a ~100-200 LOC push-to-pull adapter for scanner-rs Read-based pipeline. A memory limit MUST be set via the memlimit option to prevent 4GB dictionary allocation attacks.

Evidence: Phase 3 Deep-Dive 1 (P3.1.F1): lzma-rs HAS streaming since v0.2.0 (correcting Phase 1 claim of "one-shot only"). P3.1.F3: #![forbid(unsafe_code)], supports LZMA/LZMA2/XZ, has memlimit option. P3.1.F4: liblzma crate as C FFI fallback if perf insufficient. Phase 4 Cross-Validator: confirmed lzma-rs streaming was incorrectly dismissed. Phase 1 Agent 7 (P1.7.F1): xz decompression at 98-127 MB/s (5x slower than gzip). Phase 1 Agent 3 (P1.3.F3): CVE-2024-3094 xz backdoor — irrelevant to lzma-rs (pure Rust, not xz-utils).

## Current State

- .xz is in path policy skip set (src/git_scan/path_policy.rs — packed extension b"xz")
- .txz is in path policy skip set (src/git_scan/path_policy.rs — packed extension b"txz")
- No lzma/xz dependency in Cargo.toml
- ArchiveKind has no xz variant
- xz magic bytes: 0xFD, 0x37, 0x7A, 0x58, 0x5A, 0x00 (6 bytes)

## Desired State

- New ArchiveKind::Xz and ArchiveKind::TarXz variants
- New src/archive/formats/xz.rs module with XzStream<R>
- Extension detection: .xz → Xz, .tar.xz / .txz → TarXz
- Magic detection: 6-byte xz signature → Xz
- Memory limit enforced via lzma-rs memlimit option
- .xz/.txz REMOVED from path policy skip set
- Budget integration via CountedRead
- Simulation harness and corpus tests for xz format

## Implementation Guidance

### Dependency:
Add to Cargo.toml: `lzma-rs = { version = "0.3", features = ["stream"] }`
(Pure Rust, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], streaming since v0.2.0)

If lzma-rs performance is insufficient, fallback to: `liblzma = { version = "0.4", features = ["static"] }`
(C binding, actively maintained fork of xz2, vendors from git — CVE-2024-3094 specific attack vector does not apply)

### Files to modify:
Same dispatch-site checklist as bzip2/zstd tasks, plus:
1. `src/archive/detect.rs` — Add Xz/TarXz variants; RESTRUCTURE detect_z_suffix to handle .xz alongside .gz
2. `src/archive/formats/xz.rs` (new) — XzStream<R> with memlimit enforcement
3. All dispatch sites
4. `src/scheduler/local_fs_xz.rs` (new)
5. `src/git_scan/path_policy.rs` — Remove xz/txz from SKIP_EXTS
6. `src/sim_archive/build_xz.rs` (new) — Deterministic xz archive builder for sim harness
7. `src/sim_archive/mod.rs` — Export build_xz_bytes

### Extension detection (REQUIRES RESTRUCTURING detect_z_suffix):
Currently detect_z_suffix only handles .gz variants. Both .xz and .gz end in "z". Must restructure:
- If penultimate byte is "g" (after case-fold): existing .gz/.tgz/.tar.gz logic
- If penultimate byte is "x" (after case-fold): new .xz/.txz/.tar.xz logic
- Otherwise: None

This restructuring is the most complex part of this task. Existing unit tests + Kani proofs for detect_kind_from_name_bytes catch regressions.

### XzStream pattern (lzma-rs primary):
lzma-rs with stream feature may provide: lzma_rs::xz::read::XzDecoder<R> or a Write-based Stream. Investigate the actual API:
- If Read adapter exists: use directly like GzipStream
- If only Write-based: build a push-to-pull adapter (~100-200 LOC using internal ring buffer)

### XzStream pattern (liblzma fallback):
```rust
pub struct XzStream<R: Read> {
    dec: liblzma::read::XzDecoder<CountedRead<R>>,
    last_bytes: u64,
}
// For liblzma: Stream::new_stream_decoder(8 * 1024 * 1024, 0) for 8MB memlimit
```

### Magic detection:
6-byte sequence: 0xFD 0x37 0x7A 0x58 0x5A 0x00. First byte 0xFD — distinct from all existing formats. Longest magic sequence (6 bytes) = lowest false-positive rate.

## Simulation Harness Testing

The archive simulation harness provides deterministic end-to-end testing through the full scanner pipeline. New decompression formats MUST be wired into the sim harness.

### Required sim harness additions:

1. **Add `Xz` / `TarXz` to `ArchiveKindSpec`** (src/sim_scanner/scenario.rs).
2. **Add `build_xz_bytes`** (src/sim_archive/build_xz.rs) — deterministic xz archive materializer. Compresses payload with lzma-rs or liblzma encoder, returns bytes.
3. **Wire materialization** in `src/sim_archive/mod.rs` `materialize_archive()` match arms.
4. **Wire sim runner dispatch** in `src/sim_scanner/runner.rs` `ArchiveScanState::step()` match arms.
5. **Add to generator** in `src/sim_scanner/generator.rs` so random scenarios include xz archives.

### Required sim corpus tests (tests/simulation/scanner_archive_corpus.rs):

Follow the existing wall-clock timeout tests as templates:

```rust
// Smoke: xz archive with secret is scanned
#[test]
fn archive_xz_smoke() { ... }

// Budget: per-entry byte cap limits xz scan
#[test]
fn archive_xz_entry_byte_cap() { ... }

// Memory safety: memlimit prevents >8MB dictionary allocation
#[test]
fn archive_xz_large_dictionary_rejected() { ... }

// Wall-clock timeout via countdown (xz is 5x slower than gzip — critical)
#[test]
fn archive_xz_wall_clock_timeout_skips_later_entries() {
    run_archive_scenario_with_countdown(scenario, archive_cfg, seed, 2);
}
```

### Deterministic deadline testing with countdown:

`RunConfig.archive_deadline_countdown` (gated by `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "sim-harness"))]`) arms a deterministic countdown in `ArchiveBudgets`. Each call to `is_deadline_expired()` decrements the counter; when it hits 0 the method returns `true` without consulting the real clock. Use `run_archive_scenario_with_countdown(scenario, cfg, seed, N)` where N is the number of allowed checks before firing. This is especially important for xz at 98-127 MB/s (5x slower than gzip).

## Code References

```rust
// src/archive/detect.rs:170-220 — detect_kind_from_name_bytes + detect_z_suffix
// src/archive/formats/gzip.rs:101-182 — GzipStream template
// src/sim_archive/build_gzip.rs — gzip materializer (template for build_xz.rs)
// tests/simulation/scanner_archive_corpus.rs:860-990 — wall-clock timeout corpus test patterns
// lzma-rs crate: github.com/gendx/lzma-rs, features=["stream"]
// lzma-rs lib.rs:5 — #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
// lzma-rs Options: memlimit: Option<usize>
```

## Related Work

- scratch-bqm3: parent epic
- scratch-m1om: wall-clock timeout (prerequisite, now implemented — xz at 98-127 MB/s, needs time guard)
- scratch-gasn: bzip2 decompression task (establishes pattern; review before starting xz)
- scratch-jjzc: zstd decompression task (may modify detect.rs in parallel — coordinate)

## Acceptance Criteria

- cargo fmt --all && cargo check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings passes
- cargo test passes (including new xz unit tests)
- cargo test --features sim-harness --test simulation passes (including new xz corpus tests)
- .xz/.txz files no longer skipped by path policy
- detect_z_suffix correctly distinguishes .gz, .xz, .tar.gz, .tar.xz, .tgz, .txz (no regressions)
- detect_kind_from_name_bytes(b"file.tar.xz") returns Some(ArchiveKind::TarXz)
- sniff_kind_from_header with xz 6-byte magic returns Some(ArchiveKind::Xz)
- Secrets inside .tar.xz archives are found (smoke test)
- Wall-clock timeout works for xz streams (sim corpus test with countdown)
- Memory limit prevents >8MB dictionary allocation (unit test with crafted stream)
- No unsafe code in the XzStream implementation
- Sim harness generates random xz scenarios in scanner_archive_random tests

## Pointers

- lzma-rs crate: https://github.com/gendx/lzma-rs (Issue #97: Read/Write decoder request, Issue #101: BCJ filter support)
- lzma-rs stream feature: src/decode/stream.rs in the crate
- XZ format spec: https://tukaani.org/xz/xz-file-format.txt (Section 5.2 Security)
- liblzma crate (fallback): https://github.com/portable-network-archive/liblzma-rs
- CVE-2024-3094: NOT relevant to lzma-rs (pure Rust) or liblzma crate (builds from git, not release tarballs)
- Existing sim corpus tests: tests/simulation/scanner_archive_corpus.rs (wall_clock_timeout tests for pattern)

title: Implement CredData CSV parser and adapter
description:
## Task 4: Implement CredData CSV parser and adapter

**Priority:** P1 | **Type:** task | **Depends on:** Task 1 (scaffold)

### Why
Samsung CredData is the primary public benchmark. Its MetaRow CSV has 13 columns with CredData-specific conventions (GroundTruth codes T/F/X, colon-separated categories, -1 sentinel for ValueStart/ValueEnd).

### Files to Create
- `tools/eval-harness/src/creddata.rs`

### Files to Modify
- `tools/eval-harness/src/lib.rs` — add `pub mod creddata;`

### CredData CSV Format (13 columns)

The meta/ directory contains per-repository CSV files. Each CSV has these columns:

Id,FileID,Domain,RepoName,FilePath,LineStart,LineEnd,GroundTruth,ValueStart,ValueEnd,CryptographyKey,PredefinedPattern,Category

- FilePath: relative path within CredData corpus (starts with data/)
- LineStart, LineEnd: 1-indexed line numbers (inclusive). Constraint: LineStart <= LineEnd
- GroundTruth: "T" (true secret), "F" (false positive), "X" (test/placeholder)
- ValueStart, ValueEnd: character positions within the line; -1 means whole line
- Category: colon-separated, alphabetically-sorted rule names (e.g., "Secret:Token")

### Implementation

```rust
use crate::core::{TruthItem, TruthLabel};
use std::path::Path;

#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
struct MetaRow {
    id: String,
    #[serde(rename = "FileID")]
    file_id: String,
    domain: String,
    repo_name: String,
    file_path: String,
    line_start: i64,
    line_end: i64,
    ground_truth: String,
    value_start: i64,
    value_end: i64,
    cryptography_key: String,
    predefined_pattern: String,
    category: String,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct CredDataResult {
    pub items: Vec<TruthItem>,
    pub skipped_rows: u64,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum CredDataError {
    Io(String),
    CsvParse(String),
}

impl std::fmt::Display for CredDataError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Self::Io(e) => write!(f, "I/O error reading CredData CSV: {e}"),
            Self::CsvParse(e) => write!(f, "CSV parse error in CredData: {e}"),
        }
    }
}

pub fn parse_creddata_csv(
    meta_csv_path: &Path,
    corpus_prefix: Option<&str>,
) -> Result<CredDataResult, CredDataError> { /* ... */ }

pub fn load_creddata_meta_dir(
    meta_dir: &Path,
    corpus_prefix: Option<&str>,
) -> Result<CredDataResult, CredDataError> { /* ... */ }

fn normalize_creddata_path(raw: &str, corpus_prefix: Option<&str>) -> String { /* ... */ }
```

### Testing Strategy
- 8 unit tests: valid row parsing, missing columns, quoted fields, empty file, header-only, UTF-8 BOM, non-UTF-8 bytes, non-numeric line numbers
- 1 proptest: roundtrip serialize->parse yields identical labels
- 1 fuzz target (high priority): assert no panics on arbitrary byte input to CSV parser
- 1 integration test: 10-20 row fixture file in real CredData format at tools/eval-harness/testdata/creddata_sample.csv

### Acceptance Criteria
1. Parses CSV with T/F/X labels correctly
2. corpus_prefix stripping: normalize_creddata_path("data/repo/src/foo.py", Some("data/repo")) -> "src/foo.py"
3. Unknown GroundTruth values silently skipped and counted
4. Negative LineStart/LineEnd clamped to 0
5. load_creddata_meta_dir loads all .csv files from a directory
6. cargo clippy -- -D warnings passes
close_reason: Implemented CredData CSV parser with partial serde struct, rich counting invariant, BOM stripping, partial-success directory loading, and 19 tests (13 unit + 1 dir + 5 property). All tests pass, clippy clean.

title: Implement LeakyRepo CSV parser and adapter
description:
## Task 5: Implement LeakyRepo CSV parser and adapter

**Priority:** P1 | **Type:** task | **Depends on:** Task 1 (scaffold)

### Why
LeakyRepo is a second public benchmark using count-based comparison (per-file expected counts, not line positions).

### Files to Create
- `tools/eval-harness/src/leaky_repo.rs`

### Files to Modify
- `tools/eval-harness/src/lib.rs` — add `pub mod leaky_repo;`

### LeakyRepo secrets.csv Format

Located at .leaky-meta/secrets.csv. 3-column CSV with comment lines:

```csv
# name,num_risk,num_informative
.bash_profile,6,5
.bashrc,3,3
.docker/.dockercfg,2,2
```

- name: relative file path
- num_risk: count of actual risk lines (passwords, private keys, tokens)
- num_informative: count of potentially sensitive info lines (hostnames, usernames)
- Total expected per file = num_risk + num_informative

### Implementation

```rust
use crate::core::NormalizedFinding;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::Path;

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct FileExpectation {
    pub path: String,
    pub expected_count: u32,
    pub num_risk: u32,
    pub num_informative: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct LeakyRepoResult {
    pub file_expectations: Vec<FileExpectation>,
}

pub fn parse_leaky_repo_csv(path: &Path) -> Result<LeakyRepoResult, LeakyRepoError> { /* ... */ }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, serde::Serialize)]
pub struct FileCountComparison {
    pub path: String,
    pub expected: u32,
    pub actual: u32,
    pub tp: u32,
    pub fp: u32,
    pub fn_count: u32,
}

pub fn compare_counts(
    findings: &[NormalizedFinding],
    expectations: &[FileExpectation],
) -> Vec<FileCountComparison> { /* ... */ }
```

### Acceptance Criteria
1. Parses CSV with comment lines (# prefix) correctly
2. compare_counts: 3 expected, 5 actual -> tp=3, fp=2, fn=0
3. compare_counts: 3 expected, 1 actual -> tp=1, fp=0, fn=2
4. Empty CSV (headers only) -> empty result
5. cargo clippy -- -D warnings passes

title: Review F3: Make dedup mode explicit and remove redundant cross-rule sort
description:
## Finding: Dedup mode is implicit and cross-rule mode adds redundant sort

**Severity**: SHOULD FIX
**File(s)**: tools/eval-harness/src/finding_parser.rs, tools/eval-harness/src/main.rs, tools/eval-harness/src/matching.rs
**Type**: performance/design
**Flagged by**: Design, Performance, Complexity

### Problem
Pipeline currently does dedup_findings sort, then cross_rule_dedup_findings sort, then matching sort. Dedup semantics are encoded as call ordering instead of typed contract, increasing misuse risk and unnecessary O(n log n) work.

### Resolution Steps
1. Introduce typed dedup mode in core pipeline config.
2. Make matching config carry dedup mode and enforce valid combinations.
3. Apply dedup via one dedup entrypoint in position pipeline.
4. Ensure cross-rule mode performs only one pre-match sort.
5. Update tests for new contract.

### Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] dedup mode is explicit in config types
- [ ] cross-rule pipeline no longer performs two pre-match dedup sorts
- [ ] invalid config combinations are rejected/guarded
- [ ] cargo test passes
- [ ] cargo fmt --all && cargo check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

title: Add CharRequirements pattern validation
description:
## Problem
No way to express character-class constraints on extracted secrets. Kingfisher's PatternRequirements has min_digits, min_uppercase, min_lowercase, min_special_chars, and ignore_if_contains — used on 85+ rules. An "API key" that is all lowercase letters, or a "token" containing "EXAMPLE", passes scanner-rs but is caught by kingfisher.

## Dependencies
None formally, but naturally slots in after Task scratch-ev8e (both modify gate ordering in the same code region of window_validate.rs).

## Files to Modify

### src/api.rs (~line 752)
Add CharRequirements struct:
```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)]
pub struct CharRequirements {
    pub min_digits: u8,
    pub min_uppercase: u8,
    pub min_lowercase: u8,
    pub min_special_chars: u8,
}
```
Add serde derives if RuleSpec derives them. Check existing derives.

### src/api.rs:563 (RuleSpec struct)
Add field: pub char_requirements: Option<CharRequirements>
With #[serde(default)].

### src/rules/yaml.rs (~line 112)
Add YamlCharRequirements struct for deserialization:
```rust
#[derive(Deserialize, Default)]
struct YamlCharRequirements {
    min_digits: Option<u8>,
    min_uppercase: Option<u8>,
    min_lowercase: Option<u8>,
    min_special_chars: Option<u8>,
    ignore_if_contains: Option<Vec<String>>,
}
```

### src/rules/yaml.rs:57-98 (YamlRule struct)
Add field: char_requirements: Option<YamlCharRequirements> with #[serde(default)]

### src/rules/yaml.rs:326-413 (parse function)
Convert YamlCharRequirements → CharRequirements (api struct) + extract ignore_if_contains patterns into a separate field or bundle them together. The ignore_if_contains patterns should be compiled into PackedPatterns at rule compilation time (see rule_repr.rs below).

### src/engine/rule_repr.rs (~line 310)
Add CharReqCompiled struct:
```rust
pub(super) struct CharReqCompiled {
    pub(super) min_digits: u8,
    pub(super) min_uppercase: u8,
    pub(super) min_lowercase: u8,
    pub(super) min_special_chars: u8,
}
```

### src/engine/rule_repr.rs:393 (RuleCompiled struct)
Add field: char_requirements: u32 (gate pool index, using NO_GATE sentinel for none). Follow the same pool pattern as other gates (entropy, value_suppressors, etc.).

### src/engine/rule_repr.rs:477 (compile_rule function)
Compile char_requirements: push CharReqCompiled to gate pool, store index. Also compile ignore_if_contains into a PackedPatterns and store its pool index separately (or as a tuple with CharReqCompiled).

### src/engine/core.rs (~line 416)
Add char_req_gates pool vector to Engine (Vec<CharReqCompiled>) and a resolver method, following the pattern of other gate pools (entropy_gates, value_suppressor_gates, etc.). Also add ignore_if_contains_gates pool if storing separately.

### src/engine/helpers.rs (~line 288)
Add char_requirements_pass function:
```rust
#[inline]
pub(super) fn char_requirements_pass(bytes: &[u8], req: &CharReqCompiled) -> bool {
    let (mut digits, mut upper, mut lower, mut special) = (0u32, 0u32, 0u32, 0u32);
    for &b in bytes {
        match b {
            b'0'..=b'9' => digits += 1,
            b'A'..=b'Z' => upper += 1,
            b'a'..=b'z' => lower += 1,
            0x21..=0x2F | 0x3A..=0x40 | 0x5B..=0x60 | 0x7B..=0x7E => special += 1,
            _ => {}
        }
    }
    digits >= req.min_digits as u32
        && upper >= req.min_uppercase as u32
        && lower >= req.min_lowercase as u32
        && special >= req.min_special_chars as u32
}
```

### src/engine/window_validate.rs:84-90 (ResolvedGates struct)
Add field: char_requirements: Option<(&CharReqCompiled, Option<&PackedPatterns>)>
The tuple holds the char requirements and optional ignore_if_contains patterns.

### src/engine/window_validate.rs (resolve_gates method)
Add resolution for char_requirements from the gate pool, following existing pattern.

### src/engine/window_validate.rs (~line 497, all 4 code paths)
Insert gate check after value suppressors, before local context:
```rust
if let Some((creq, ignore_pats)) = gates.char_requirements {
    if let Some(pats) = ignore_pats {
        if contains_any_memmem(secret_bytes, pats) {
            return;
        }
    }
    if !char_requirements_pass(secret_bytes, creq) {
        return;
    }
}
```
Apply this in all 4 paths (raw, utf16, raw_into, utf16_into).

### default_rules.yaml
Add char_requirements to high-impact rules:
- generic-api-key: { min_digits: 1, min_uppercase: 1, ignore_if_contains: ["EXAMPLE", "TEST", "SAMPLE", "DUMMY"] }
- aws-access-key-id (if exists): { min_digits: 2, ignore_if_contains: ["EXAMPLE", "TEST"] }
- aws-secret-access-key (if exists): { min_digits: 3, ignore_if_contains: ["EXAMPLE", "TEST"] }
- private-key: { min_digits: 4 } (real PEM keys always have digits in the base64 body)

### docs/data-types.md
Add CharRequirements class diagram.

### docs/detection-rules.md
Add char_requirements to YAML schema docs with examples.

### docs/engine-window-validation.md
Add gate to sequence diagram (after value suppressors, before local context).

## ignore_if_contains Implementation Note
ignore_if_contains maps to the same PackedPatterns + contains_any_memmem infrastructure already used by value_suppressors_any. The only difference: ignore_if_contains is defined in char_requirements YAML block. At compile time, it gets its own PackedPatterns instance in the gate pool. Look at how value_suppressors are compiled in rule_repr.rs and follow the same pattern.

## Testing
1. Unit test for char_requirements_pass with known byte strings (all digits, mixed, empty).
2. Integration test: rule with min_digits: 2, secret with 0 digits → rejected.
3. Integration test: ignore_if_contains: ["EXAMPLE"], secret AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE → rejected.
4. Integration test: secret with sufficient character diversity → passes.
5. YAML round-trip test with char_requirements present and absent.
6. cargo test --all + cargo bench.

## Performance
O(n) single pass over 10-150 bytes — cheaper than entropy. ignore_if_contains uses memmem (O(n*m) worst case, but patterns are short and few). Runs only on findings that passed regex + entropy. Negligible overhead.

## Validation
cargo fmt --all && cargo check && cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

title: Fix write_f64 overflow on large finite inputs
description:
## Context
PR #80 made low-level JSON write helpers public and benches now call `write_f64` directly (`src/unified/json_write.rs`).

Current implementation:
- casts `abs` to `u64` (`let mut integer = abs as u64`)
- computes `frac` from `(abs - integer as f64) * 100.0`
- carries with `integer += 1` when `frac >= 100`

For large finite values (e.g. `1e20`), `abs as u64` saturates to `u64::MAX`, and `frac` can also saturate, so `integer += 1` overflows.

Repro (debug): panic `attempt to add with overflow`
Repro (optimized): wraps and emits invalid numeric text semantics.

## Goal
Make `write_f64` robust for all finite `f64` inputs (no panic, no wraparound, always valid JSON numeric output with 2 decimals).

## Scope
- Update overflow/carry handling in `write_f64`
- Add targeted tests for large finite magnitudes (including values above `u64::MAX as f64`)
- Keep existing NaN/Inf fallback behavior unchanged unless intentionally redesigned

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `write_f64(1e20, &mut buf)` does not panic in debug builds
- [ ] release behavior does not wrap integer component
- [ ] output remains well-formed with exactly two fractional digits
- [ ] tests added for boundary values around `u64::MAX as f64`
- [ ] existing `json_write` tests remain green

## Notes
This is a pre-merge blocker for PR #80 because it is a correctness bug in a public helper.
close_reason: Implemented robust write_f64 clamping for large finite inputs; added boundary regression test; validated via cargo check + targeted test

title: Git attribution: emit deduped commit_meta dictionary keyed by commit_id
description:
## Context
After wiring `commit_id` into finding events, repeating commit metadata on every finding wastes bytes and CPU (OID hex formatting, repeated serialization). `scanner-rs` already has O(1) commit metadata lookup via `CommitGraphIndex`.

Relevant primitives:
- `CommitGraphIndex::commit_oid()` and `CommitGraphIndex::committer_timestamp()` (`src/git_scan/commit_graph.rs`).
- Existing finding event already carries `commit_id` (`src/unified/events.rs`).
- Existing lock-free dedupe primitive: `AtomicBitSet` (`src/stdx/atomic_bitset.rs`).

## Goal
Add a deduped commit metadata side channel/table keyed by `commit_id` so findings stay compact while still exposing commit OID/time.

## Scope
- Introduce a `commit_meta` event/table emitted once per commit ID encountered in findings.
- Include at least:
  - `commit_id` (u32 graph position)
  - `commit_oid` (raw bytes or canonical hex representation)
  - `committer_timestamp` (u64 epoch seconds)
- Keep finding events compact (do not duplicate OID/time per finding).

## Performance Constraints
- Emit-once guarantee under concurrency using atomic bitset gating.
- O(1) lookup from commit_id -> metadata via precomputed arrays.
- Avoid per-finding OID formatting and repeated allocation.
- Keep serialization in manual writer path; avoid introducing dynamic JSON alloc churn in hot loop.
- Target regression: statistically insignificant at repo-scale (<1-2%), with p50/p95 checks.

## Data-Structure/Algorithm Notes
- Dense membership: atomic bitset sized to `CommitGraphIndex::len()`.
- Metadata storage: SoA-leaning representation for cache locality (packed OIDs + timestamp vecs; avoid scattered heap objects).
- Sink path should accept dictionary-style metadata emission for downstream join by `commit_id`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every commit ID appearing in findings has exactly one matching `commit_meta` emission.
- No duplicate `commit_meta` under parallel scanning.
- Findings remain compact and reference commit metadata by ID.
- JSONL/text/sarif behavior documented for new metadata channel.
- Perf evidence included: before/after throughput and output size deltas.
notes:
Research refinement (implementation-critical):
- Add explicit determinism contract for `commit_meta` side-channel emission.
- `AtomicBitSet` emit-once gating solves duplication, but does not guarantee stable output order under parallel workers.
- Require either:
  1) buffered + sorted `commit_meta` flush (e.g., by `commit_id`), or
  2) documented non-deterministic stream order with deterministic key semantics for downstream joins.
- Include acceptance test for no duplicates + expected ordering semantics.

title: Unify top-level and nested gzip chunk pipelines
description:
Follow-up from PR #97 (consolidation-only): this is a maintainability/design task, not a regression fix.

## Problem
`src/scheduler/local_fs_gzip.rs` still has two implementations of the same chunk-scan pipeline:
- Top-level gzip path in `process_gzip_file` (`src/scheduler/local_fs_gzip.rs:185` onward)
- Nested gzip path using `scan_and_emit_chunk` (`src/scheduler/local_fs_gzip.rs:355` onward)

Only the nested path was migrated to the shared helper. The top-level path still inlines scan->drop-prefix->drain->dedupe->emit->metrics logic.

## Why this matters
Behavior can drift when only one path is updated (dedupe, dropped-finding accounting, emit ordering, metrics semantics, offset/carry bookkeeping).

## Concrete examples
If we later change `account_effective_dropped_findings(...)` or event/persistence emission ordering in one path and forget the other, top-level and nested gzip scans can diverge for identical payloads.

## Desired outcome
- Use one canonical implementation for the chunk processing stage in both gzip paths.
- Preserve existing behavior and metrics values.
- Keep hot-path overhead zero/near-zero (no dynamic dispatch).

## Code references
- `src/scheduler/local_fs_gzip.rs:185`
- `src/scheduler/local_fs_gzip.rs:355`
- `src/scheduler/local_fs_archive_ctx.rs:267`

## Non-goals
- No broad redesign of tar/zip loops in this task.
- No behavior changes to budget charging logic.

title: Add digit-only entropy penalty for hex rules
description:
## Overview

When an extracted secret from a hex-based rule contains only ASCII digits [0-9], apply an entropy penalty before the threshold check. Targets phone numbers, timestamps, version strings, and numeric IDs that frequently pass naive entropy thresholds.

## Motivation

All-digit sequences like "20240215143052789012" (timestamp-like) have Shannon entropy ~3.3 bits/byte, passing a typical 3.0 hex threshold. But they are never secrets.

**Evidence**: detect-secrets implements this exact heuristic in high_entropy_strings.py (Level 3). 3 research agents independently identified digit-only FPs.

## Implementation

### Penalty formula (from detect-secrets)

```rust
fn apply_digit_penalty(entropy: f64, bytes: &[u8]) -> f64 {
    if bytes.iter().all(|&b| b.is_ascii_digit()) {
        let penalty = 1.2 / (bytes.len() as f64).log2();
        entropy - penalty
    } else {
        entropy
    }
}
```

For 20-char all-digit string: penalty = 1.2 / log2(20) ~ 0.278 bits/byte
- Before: 3.32 bits/byte (passes 3.0) -> After: 3.04 bits/byte
- For 10-char: penalty ~ 0.361 (stronger for shorter strings)
- For 40-char: penalty ~ 0.226

### Files to modify

1. **src/api.rs** (EntropySpec at line 726): Add field digit_penalty: bool (default false)
2. **src/engine/helpers.rs** (entropy_gate_passes at line 274): After computing Shannon entropy, if digit_penalty enabled, check all-digit and apply penalty
3. **src/engine/rule_repr.rs**: Add compiled digit_penalty flag
4. **src/rules/yaml.rs**: Parse digit_penalty boolean
5. **default_rules.yaml**: Enable on hex-based rules

### All-digit check
Cost: ~1 comparison per byte, short-circuits on first non-digit. ~10-30ns for 32 bytes.

### Numerical examples
- "31415926535897932384" (20 digits, pi): entropy=3.22, penalty=0.278, adjusted=2.94 -> REJECTED at 3.0
- "9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d" (20 hex, mixed): no penalty -> unchanged
- "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE" (AWS key): no penalty (has letters) -> unchanged

### Risk analysis
- Only apply to rules with digit_penalty: true (opt-in per rule)
- Never apply to non-hex patterns (base64, alphanumeric tokens)
- detect-secrets has used this in production at Yelp for years

### References
- detect-secrets high_entropy_strings.py
- Empirical: phone numbers, timestamps, numeric IDs are top FP source for hex rules

title: Add SIMD character-class profiler pre-filter gate
description:
## Overview

Add a new pre-filter gate between keywords and regex that classifies each byte in the candidate window into 4 classes (uppercase, lowercase, digit, special) using SIMD vpshufb/vqtbl1q technique, then rejects windows whose character-class distribution is clearly not secret-shaped.

## Motivation

Windows >90% lowercase with <2% digits are English prose, not secrets. Rejecting before expensive regex saves significant time. The vpshufb nibble-lookup is proven at GB/s scale in simdjson. scanner-rs already uses vqtbl1q_u8 in transform.rs:1254 for base64 classification.

**Evidence**: Level 5. simdjson, Hyperscan use this. 2 research agents identified independently.

## Implementation

### SIMD byte classification (NEON)

```rust
#[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")]
unsafe fn classify_16_bytes_neon(bytes: &[u8; 16]) -> [u32; 4] {
    use std::arch::aarch64::*;
    let lo_lut = vld1q_u8(LO_NIBBLE_TABLE.as_ptr());
    let hi_lut = vld1q_u8(HI_NIBBLE_TABLE.as_ptr());
    let input = vld1q_u8(bytes.as_ptr());
    let lo = vandq_u8(input, vdupq_n_u8(0x0F));
    let hi = vshrq_n_u8(input, 4);
    let lo_class = vqtbl1q_u8(lo_lut, lo);
    let hi_class = vqtbl1q_u8(hi_lut, hi);
    let result = vandq_u8(lo_class, hi_class);
    count_classes(result) // [upper, lower, digit, special]
}
```

### Gate logic

```rust
fn char_class_gate_passes(profile: &CharClassProfile, spec: &CharClassSpec) -> bool {
    if profile.lower_ratio > spec.max_lower_ratio { return false; }
    let mixed = profile.upper_ratio + profile.digit_ratio + profile.special_ratio;
    if mixed < spec.min_mixed_ratio { return false; }
    true
}
```

### Recommended thresholds (conservative)
- max_lower_ratio: 0.95 (reject >95% lowercase only)
- min_mixed_ratio: 0.05 (require at least 5% non-lowercase)

### Files to modify

1. **New file: src/engine/simd_classify.rs**: SIMD classification with NEON + SSE2/AVX2 + scalar fallback
2. **src/engine/window_validate.rs**: Add char-class gate before regex
3. **src/api.rs** (RuleSpec): Add optional CharClassSpec
4. **src/engine/rule_repr.rs**: Compiled char-class gate in RuleCompiled
5. **src/engine/core.rs**: Char-class gate pool in Engine
6. **src/engine/mod.rs**: Export new module

### Architecture
- Process 16-byte (NEON) or 32-byte (AVX2) chunks
- Scalar fallback for <16 byte windows
- Operates on FULL candidate window, not just extracted secret
- Cost: ~0.2-0.5ns/byte = ~10-30ns for 64-byte window

### Risk analysis
- Conservative thresholds minimize false negatives
- Gate must be optional per-rule
- Benchmark SIMD vs scalar for typical window sizes (20-200 bytes)

### References
- Langdale & Lemire, "Parsing Gigabytes of JSON per Second" (arXiv:1902.08318)
- scanner-rs transform.rs:1254 (existing vqtbl1q_u8)
- scanner-rs json_write.rs (existing SIMD escape classification)

title: Implement finding-to-truth matching logic
description:
## Task 7: Implement finding-to-truth matching logic

**Priority:** P1 | **Type:** task | **Depends on:** Tasks 1 (scaffold), 2 (line_index), 5 (leaky_repo)

### Why
Core evaluation logic classifying each (finding, truth) pair into TP/FP/FN/Unlabeled. Handles position-based matching (CredData/synthetic) and count-based matching (LeakyRepo).

### Files to Create
- `tools/eval-harness/src/matching.rs`

### Files to Modify
- `tools/eval-harness/src/lib.rs` — add `pub mod matching;`

### Matching Algorithm (Position-Based)

For each finding:
1. Convert byte range [byte_start, byte_end) to line numbers using LineIndex built from file contents
2. Look up truth items with the same path
3. Check line overlap: finding lines overlap truth item lines
4. (Optional) Check rule match: finding rule name appears in truth item's colon-separated category
5. Classify: Positive truth -> TP, Negative/Placeholder truth -> FP, no match -> Unlabeled
6. Unmatched Positive truth items -> FN

Each truth item can match at most one finding (greedy first-match). Each finding matches at most one truth item.

### Implementation

```rust
use crate::core::{MatchClass, NormalizedFinding, TruthItem, TruthLabel};
use crate::line_index::LineIndex;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::PathBuf;

#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct MatchResult {
    pub finding_classes: Vec<(NormalizedFinding, MatchClass)>,
    pub false_negatives: Vec<TruthItem>,
    pub tp: u64,
    pub fp: u64,
    pub fn_count: u64,
    pub unlabeled: u64,
}

pub struct MatchConfig {
    pub require_rule_match: bool,
    pub corpus_root: PathBuf,
}

pub fn match_position_based(
    findings: &[NormalizedFinding],
    truth: &[TruthItem],
    config: &MatchConfig,
) -> MatchResult { /* ... lazy line index building, greedy matching ... */ }
```

### Testing Strategy
- 8 unit tests: exact line match TP, same line different rule FP, adjacent line FN, multiline overlap, duplicate findings, no findings (all FN), no labels (all Unlabeled), empty inputs
- 5 proptest properties: conservation of findings (TP+FP+Unlabeled==len(findings)), conservation of labels (TP+FN==positive_truth), precision/recall bounded [0,1], adding correct finding doesn't decrease recall, determinism
- 1 integration test: golden-file with small synthetic corpus

### Acceptance Criteria
1. Finding at bytes overlapping truth line -> TP if Positive label
2. No line overlap -> Unlabeled
3. Rule match: "aws-access-key-id" matches category "aws-access-key-id:Token" (colon-split, case-insensitive)
4. Count-based: 3 expected, 5 actual -> TP=3, FP=2, FN=0
5. Missing file -> Unlabeled
6. cargo clippy -- -D warnings passes
notes:
## Research-Driven Additions

### A. Corrections Overlay for Label Noise

**Research basis:**
- Northcutt et al. 2021 "Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets" (arxiv:2103.14749) [evidence 4]: Major ML benchmarks average 3.3% label errors. Model rankings flipped after correction. Single-annotator secret detection benchmarks likely have higher rates (5-8%).
- SecretBench: 68% of candidates in vaguely-defined "Other" category, only 0.8% labeled true. No inter-annotator agreement. [P1.3.F1]
- FPSecretBench: README states "may contain mislabeled true positives." DPA requirement confirms some "FPs" are real secrets. [P1.3.F2]
- CredData: 3-label scheme (T/F/X) with documented ground rules but no IAA. Policy: test-directory credentials labeled True. [P1.3.F3]
- git-secrets (awslabs): Uses .gitallowed file to override false positives. Direct model for a corrections overlay. [P1.3.F6]
- Cross-benchmark disagreement: CredData labels test-dir creds as True; SecretBench may not. Items where benchmarks disagree should auto-Placeholder. [P1.3.F7]

**New file:** tools/eval-harness/src/corrections.rs

**Format (TOML):**

    # corrections.toml — label overrides applied after corpus loading
    [[corrections]]
    path = "data/repo42/src/config.py"
    line_start = 15
    line_end = 15
    rule = "aws-access-key-id"           # optional
    corrected_label = "Negative"          # Positive | Negative | Placeholder
    reason = "example key from AWS docs"  # human-readable

**Implementation outline:**

    pub struct CorrectionsOverlay {
        map: HashMap<(String, u32, u32), TruthLabel>,
    }

    impl CorrectionsOverlay {
        pub fn load(path: &Path) -> Result<Self, ...> { /* parse TOML */ }
        pub fn apply(&self, truth: &mut [TruthItem]) {
            for item in truth.iter_mut() {
                let key = (item.path.clone(), item.line_start, item.line_end);
                if let Some(label) = self.map.get(&key) {
                    item.label = *label;
                }
            }
        }
    }

**Integration:** Called in match_position_based() before classification loop. CLI arg: --corrections <path> (optional, passed through MatchConfig).

**Tests:**
- Apply correction Positive->Negative: finding changes from TP to FP
- Apply correction to Placeholder: finding becomes Unlabeled
- No-match correction: truth items unchanged
- Proptest: corrections never change item count, only labels

### B. Per-Rule FN Counts

**Research basis:**
- sklearn multi-label average_precision_score, OWASP per-category scoring [P1.2.F5]
- Current RuleMetrics has false_neg/recall/f1 fields but always zero (metrics.rs:84-87)
- Per-rule AP exposes which rules have well-calibrated confidence
- CredData Category field (colon-separated, e.g. "Secret:Token") maps to rules

**Implementation:** In match_position_based(), track unmatched truth items per rule:

    // In MatchResult, add:
    pub fn_by_rule: HashMap<String, u64>,

    // After matching loop, unmatched Positive truth items:
    for truth in unmatched_positives {
        if let Some(rule) = truth.rule.as_ref() {
            *fn_by_rule.entry(rule.clone()).or_default() += 1;
        }
    }

Then merge fn_by_rule into per_rule RuleMetrics in compute_metrics.

**Caveat:** Rules with <5 TP produce unstable per-rule AP. Add minimum sample threshold.

**Tests:**
- 3 truth items for rule_a, 2 matched: fn_by_rule["rule_a"] == 1
- Rule with all matches: false_neg == 0, recall == 1.0
- Rule with no matches: false_neg == N, recall == 0.0

### References
1. Northcutt et al. 2021 — arxiv:2103.14749 — pervasive label errors
2. Northcutt et al. 2019 — arxiv:1911.00068 — confident learning
3. SecretBench — github.com/setu1421/SecretBench
4. FPSecretBench — github.com/setu1421/FPSecretBench
5. CredData — github.com/Samsung/CredData
6. git-secrets — github.com/awslabs/git-secrets

title: Git attribution: lazy author/committer identity enrichment with string interning
description:
## Context
Commit graph does not carry author/committer names/emails. Emitting identity fields requires commit object parsing, which can be expensive if done eagerly for all commits.

Need a lazy strategy:
- Parse commit objects only for commit IDs that actually appear in findings.
- Preserve hot-path characteristics of scanner.

## Goal
Add lazy identity enrichment (author/committer name/email) with minimal memory and CPU overhead.

## Scope
- Extend commit metadata pipeline to support optional identity enrichment.
- Parse commit objects on demand for “referenced by finding” commits only.
- Intern strings into pooled storage and emit dictionary refs (`u32` IDs) instead of repeating full strings.

## Performance Constraints
- Zero impact when identity enrichment is disabled.
- Bounded overhead when enabled:
  - Parse only referenced commits.
  - Cache parsed commit identities to avoid repeat decode.
  - No per-finding string clone.
- Use compact interning strategy (byte arena + index table) to reduce alloc pressure.

## Data-Structure/Algorithm Notes
- Candidate design: intern pool with
  - `Vec<u8>` byte arena
  - `(offset,len)` entries
  - hash map for dedupe to stable `u32` intern IDs
- Metadata emission should expose intern IDs + optional dictionary section to support downstream resolution.

## Correctness Notes
- Handle malformed commit headers robustly (invalid UTF-8, missing fields, odd signatures).
- Ensure author/committer field parsing obeys git object format semantics and remains format-agnostic (sha1/sha256 repos).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Identity data emitted only for commits referenced by findings.
- Repeated identities are interned and not duplicated in output payload.
- Fallback behavior defined for parse failures (no panic; partial metadata allowed).
- Benchmark includes CPU + memory deltas with enrichment off/on.
notes:
Research refinement (decision gate):
- Treat identity strategy as an A/B benchmarked choice, not a fixed design.
- Reason specific to scanner-rs: commit objects are already parsed during commit-graph acquisition path (`artifact_acquire -> commit_loader -> parse_commit`), so eager extraction may be cheaper than assumed.
- Required benchmark comparison:
  1) eager identity extraction+interning during commit load
  2) lazy ODB re-parse for finding-referenced commits only
- Decide based on measured CPU/memory on representative repos; record winner and rationale in issue notes.

title: Add XOR filter for known false-positive dictionary
description:
## Overview

Build a BinaryFuse8 XOR filter at engine construction from a curated dictionary of known false-positive secret values (placeholder tokens, example keys, sequential strings). Use as a confidence penalty signal (not hard suppression) during post-regex validation.

## Motivation

Existing value_suppressors use linear memmem scanning. For large FP dictionaries (hundreds+ entries), O(1) probabilistic lookup is faster and more scalable. XOR filters use 30-40% less memory than bloom filters for static sets.

**Evidence**: Level 4. Graf & Lemire (arXiv:1912.08258). xorf crate (1.7M downloads). 2 agents recommended.

## Implementation

### XOR filter construction (engine build time)

```rust
use xorf::BinaryFuse8;
use ahash::AHasher;

let fp_hashes: Vec<u64> = FP_DICTIONARY.iter()
    .map(|entry| hash_normalized(entry))
    .collect();
let filter = BinaryFuse8::try_from(&fp_hashes)?;
// filter.contains(&hash) -> bool, ~43ns lookup
// Memory: ~9 bits/entry = ~11KB for 10K entries
```

### FP dictionary categories
1. Placeholder tokens: "EXAMPLE_KEY", "changeme", "test_api_key_12345", "TODO_REPLACE"
2. Common test values: "password123", "test1234", "dummy_token"
3. Sequential strings: "abcdefghijklmnop", "0123456789abcdef"
4. Documentation examples: "sk_test_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX", "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"
5. Known UUIDs: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
6. Redaction markers: "REDACTED", "REMOVED", "CENSORED"
7. Expanded from existing SAFELIST_SECRET_BYTES_PATTERNS

### Integration

```rust
// In window_validate.rs, after regex + secret extraction:
let secret_hash = ahash_of(normalized(extracted_secret));
if engine.fp_filter.contains(&secret_hash) {
    confidence -= 3; // soft signal, NOT hard suppression
}
```

### Files to modify

1. **New file: src/engine/fp_filter.rs**: Dictionary + XOR filter construction
2. **src/engine/core.rs** (Engine at line 266): Add fp_filter: Option<BinaryFuse8>
3. **src/engine/window_validate.rs**: XOR filter check after regex match
4. **Cargo.toml**: Add xorf = "0.12"

### Key decisions
- **Soft signal only**: 0.4% FPP means ~4/1000 real secrets get penalized. Unacceptable for hard rejection. Confidence penalty only.
- **Hash normalization**: lowercase + trim before hashing
- **Static set**: Built once at engine construction. Immutable.
- **ahash**: Already a dependency, ~5ns/hash

### Numerical analysis
- 10K entries: ~11KB, ~43ns lookup
- 100K entries: ~110KB, ~43ns (same!)
- FPP 0.39%: acceptable as soft signal

### References
- Graf & Lemire arXiv:1912.08258
- xorf: https://docs.rs/xorf/latest/xorf/
- TruffleHog fp_badlist.txt, fp_words.txt, fp_uuids.txt

title: Hoist per-item buffer allocation to ConnectorCpuRunner
description:
## Context
Code review of PR #160 (connector pipeline item-level read/scan).

## Current State
Both `stream_item_via_open()` (line 415) and `stream_item_via_range_read()` (line 466) in `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs` allocate a fresh zeroed buffer per item:
```rust
let mut buf = vec![0_u8; overlap.saturating_add(cfg.chunk_size)];
```
The buffer size is constant for the entire run (`overlap + chunk_size`), so this allocation is repeated unnecessarily for every item on every page.

## Desired State
The buffer should be allocated once (either in `ConnectorCpuRunner::new()` or in the `scan_connector` dispatch closure) and reused across all items. This eliminates heap allocation overhead, zeroing cost, and memory fragmentation for high-item-count pages.

## Implementation Guidance
- Add a `buf: Vec<u8>` field to `ConnectorCpuRunner` or create an `ItemScanContext` struct
- Initialize once with `vec![0_u8; overlap + chunk_size]`
- Pass `&mut buf` into streaming functions instead of allocating locally
- This also addresses the `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` smell — grouping `connector`, `cpu_runner`, `metrics`, `cfg`, `overlap`, and `buf` into a context struct reduces 7+ params to 3

## Code References
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:415` — `stream_item_via_open` allocation
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:466` — `stream_item_via_range_read` allocation
- `src/scheduler/connector_pipeline.rs:290-305` — `ConnectorCpuRunner` struct

## Related Work
Matches the scratch reuse pattern already used in `ConnectorCpuRunner` (line 301: `Vec::with_capacity(engine.max_findings_per_chunk())`).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Buffer allocated once per scan run, not per item
- [ ] Both open and range_read paths share the same buffer
- [ ] `cargo test -p scanner-rs --lib` passes
- [ ] `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` clean
- [ ] `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean
close_reason: Buffer hoist already implemented: buf/overlap/chunk_size are fields on ConnectorCpuRunner, allocated once in new()

title: Expand offline structural validation (npm, PyPI, Slack, Twilio, GitLab, Stripe)
description:
## Overview

Expand offline_validate.rs to support structural validation for more token types beyond current 5 (GitHub PAT, Grafana, AWS, Sentry, generic CRC32/Base62). Each new validator provides near-zero FP for its token type.

## Motivation

Structural validation is the single highest-ROI FP reduction technique. GitHub engineering blog: "A checksum virtually eliminates false positives for secret scanning offline." 4 out of 5 research agents independently identified this as top priority.

**Evidence**: Level 5, proven at scale across GitHub, AWS, Grafana, Sentry.

## Candidate token types

### 1. npm tokens (npm_XXXX)
- Prefix: "npm_" (4 bytes)
- Validation: prefix + base64 validity + length constraints

### 2. PyPI tokens (pypi-XXXX)
- Prefix: "pypi-" (5 bytes)
- Validation: prefix + base64url decode validity

### 3. Slack tokens (xoxb-, xoxp-, xapp-, xoxs-)
- Prefixes: "xoxb-", "xoxp-", "xapp-", "xoxs-" (5 bytes each)
- Validation: prefix + segment structure (hyphen-separated numeric + alphanumeric)
- Length: typically 50-80 chars

### 4. Stripe tokens (sk_live_, pk_live_, sk_test_, pk_test_)
- Prefixes: "sk_live_", "pk_live_", etc. (8 bytes)
- Validation: prefix + alphanumeric suffix + expected length (24 chars after prefix)

### 5. Twilio tokens
- Prefix: "SK" or "AC" (2 bytes) + 32 hex chars
- Validation: prefix + exactly 32 hex characters

### 6. GitLab tokens (glpat-)
- Prefix: "glpat-" (6 bytes)
- Validation: prefix + alphanumeric suffix + length

## Implementation pattern

Follow existing pattern in src/engine/offline_validate.rs:

```rust
// Add new variants to OfflineValidationSpec enum in src/api.rs:767
pub enum OfflineValidationSpec {
    // ... existing ...
    NpmToken,
    PyPiToken,
    SlackToken,
    StripeToken,
    TwilioApiKey,
    GitLabPat,
}
```

### Files to modify

1. **src/api.rs** (OfflineValidationSpec at line 767): Add new enum variants
2. **src/engine/offline_validate.rs** (validate at line 75): Add match arms + validation functions
3. **src/rules/yaml.rs** (convert_offline_validation at line 276): Add YAML tag -> spec mapping
4. **default_rules.yaml**: Annotate matching rules with offline_validation specs
5. **Tests**: Unit tests per validator (valid, invalid, wrong length, wrong prefix, indeterminate)

### Key design principle
Return Indeterminate (not Invalid) when format is ambiguous. Only return Invalid when check definitively proves token is malformed (e.g., CRC mismatch). Each validator is ~50-100 lines + tests, independent of others.

### Priority order
Slack and Stripe first (most common in codebases), then npm/PyPI/GitLab/Twilio.

### References
- GitHub engineering blog on token format design
- Slack docs: https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/tokens
- Stripe docs: https://docs.stripe.com/keys
- GitLab docs: https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/profile/personal_access_tokens.html

title: Clarify cache insert semantics on key-hit
description:
Follow-up from PR #97 (consolidation-only): clarify semantics of cache insertion on key hit.

## Problem
`SetAssociativeCache::insert` treats an existing-key hit as:
- refresh clock bit
- update metadata via `update_existing(args)`
- **does not rewrite payload bytes**

Reference: `src/git_scan/cache_common.rs:253`

For a generic reusable cache API, this can be surprising because method name `insert` often implies writing/replacing value bytes.

## Why this matters
Future cache users may assume key-hit `insert` updates bytes and accidentally rely on stale payload content.

## Desired outcome
Pick and document one explicit contract:
1. Keep behavior, but rename/split API (`insert_or_refresh`, `refresh_existing`, `insert_new`) and make docs unambiguous, or
2. Change behavior to rewrite bytes on key-hit and adjust callers/tests.

## Concrete examples
Current key-hit path:
```rust
if slot.base().valid && slot.matches_key(key) {
    slot.base_mut().clock = 1;
    slot.update_existing(args);
    return true;
}
```

## Code references
- `src/git_scan/cache_common.rs:237`
- `src/git_scan/cache_common.rs:253`
- `src/git_scan/tree_cache.rs:141`
- `src/git_scan/tree_delta_cache.rs:204`

## Non-goals
- No unsafe/lifetime redesign in this task.
acceptance_criteria: Chosen contract is explicit in API/docs/tests; cache callers use the clarified behavior.

title: Implement PRC-AUC and metrics computation
description:
## Task 8: Implement PRC-AUC and metrics computation

**Priority:** P1 | **Type:** task | **Depends on:** Task 1 (scaffold)

### Why
Primary quality metric is PRC-AUC (Average Precision), computed via the step-function formula (NOT trapezoidal, which overestimates for imbalanced data per Davis & Goadrich 2006).

### Files to Create
- `tools/eval-harness/src/metrics.rs`

### Files to Modify
- `tools/eval-harness/src/lib.rs` — add `pub mod metrics;`

### PRC-AUC Algorithm (Average Precision)

AP = sum_n [ (recall[n] - recall[n-1]) * precision[n] ]

1. Collect only TP and FP findings (skip Unlabeled)
2. Sort by confidence descending (ties: TP before FP)
3. Walk sorted list, maintain running TP and FP counts
4. At each step: precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / total_positives
5. Sum (recall[n] - recall[n-1]) * precision[n] when recall changes
6. Baseline (random) = total_positives / (total_positives + total_negatives)

Why NOT trapezoidal: Linear interpolation between PR points is incorrect because precision is a non-linear function of recall. The step function (AP) is conservative and standard in IR evaluation.

### Implementation

```rust
use crate::core::{MatchClass, NormalizedFinding};
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
pub struct EvalMetrics {
    pub precision_recall_auc: f64,
    pub precision: f64,
    pub recall: f64,
    pub f1: f64,
    pub tp: u64,
    pub fp: u64,
    pub false_neg: u64,
    pub unlabeled: u64,
    pub baseline_ap: f64,
    pub per_rule: BTreeMap<String, RuleMetrics>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
pub struct RuleMetrics {
    pub tp: u64,
    pub fp: u64,
    pub false_neg: u64,
    pub precision: f64,
    pub recall: f64,
    pub f1: f64,
}

pub fn compute_metrics(
    classified: &[(NormalizedFinding, MatchClass)],
    fn_count: u64,
    total_positives: u64,
) -> EvalMetrics { /* ... */ }

fn compute_average_precision(
    classified: &[(NormalizedFinding, MatchClass)],
    total_positives: u64,
) -> f64 { /* ... step-function AP ... */ }

fn compute_per_rule(classified: &[(NormalizedFinding, MatchClass)]) -> BTreeMap<String, RuleMetrics> { /* ... */ }

fn safe_div(num: f64, den: f64) -> f64 {
    if den == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { num / den }
}
```

### Testing Strategy
- 8 oracle tests: perfect classifier (AP=1.0), worst (AP=0.0), 50% classifier, known 5-point curve (hand-computed), single point, all-negative predictions, zero-TP (no NaN), tied scores
- 6 proptest properties: AP bounded [0,1], AP always finite, perfect ranking => AP=1.0, F1 bounded [0,1], F1 <= arithmetic mean(P,R), tied scores produce finite AP

### Acceptance Criteria
1. Perfect classifier: precision_recall_auc == 1.0, precision == 1.0, recall == 1.0
2. Worst classifier: precision_recall_auc == 0.0, precision == 0.0
3. Known 5-point curve hand-computed value matches within epsilon
4. Empty input: all metrics are 0.0, no NaN
5. cargo clippy -- -D warnings passes
notes:
## Research-Driven Additions (from deeper-research evaluation)

### A. Precision-at-Fixed-Recall and Recall-at-Fixed-Precision

**Research basis:**
- sklearn precision_recall_curve docs, Neptune.ai evaluation guide [evidence 3]
- P@R answers "what precision if I catch 95% of secrets?" — directly actionable for deployment. R@P answers "what recall at ≤5% FP rate?" — for alert-fatigue budgets.
- Coralogix PR-AUC guide recommends reporting P@R=0.90/0.95 and R@P=0.95 as "ops-friendly thresholds" alongside aggregate AP.

**Implementation outline:**

Add to EvalMetrics struct:

    pub precision_at_recall: Vec<(f64, Option<f64>)>,  // [(target_r, p)]
    pub recall_at_precision: Vec<(f64, Option<f64>)>,   // [(target_p, r)]

Extract PR curve points from compute_average_precision into a reusable fn:

    struct PrPoint { precision: f64, recall: f64, confidence: i8 }

    fn build_pr_curve(classified, total_positives) -> Vec<PrPoint>
    // Same sort + tie-collapse logic as compute_average_precision
    // but returns the operating points instead of summing AP

    fn precision_at_recall(curve: &[PrPoint], target: f64) -> Option<f64>
    // Walk curve from high-recall end. Find first point where recall >= target.
    // Return precision at that point. None if target > max achievable recall.

    fn recall_at_precision(curve: &[PrPoint], target: f64) -> Option<f64>
    // Walk curve from high-recall end. Find highest recall where precision >= target.

Default targets: P@R={0.80, 0.90, 0.95}, R@P=0.95.

**Caveat:** With i8 confidence (11 discrete levels 0-10), PR curve has at most 11 operating points. Values are piecewise-constant. Still informative for deployment thresholds.

**Tests to add:**
- Perfect classifier: P@R=0.95 returns Some(1.0)
- All FP: P@R=0.95 returns None
- Known 5-point curve: hand-verify P@R and R@P values
- Proptest: P@R result (when Some) is in [0.0, 1.0]
- Proptest: R@P result (when Some) is in [0.0, 1.0]

### B. Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for AP

**Research basis:**
- Saito & Rehmsmeier, "The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot..." (PLOS ONE 2015) [evidence 4, peer-reviewed]
- Without CIs, AP change 0.87->0.89 between versions could be noise. CIs answer "did the scanner actually improve?" — essential for regression gating.
- MLPerf uses fixed seeds + bootstrap for cross-submission comparison.

**Implementation outline:**

    pub struct BootstrapConfig {
        pub n_iterations: u32,  // default 1000
        pub alpha: f64,         // default 0.05 (95% CI)
        pub seed: u64,          // default 42, deterministic
    }

    pub fn bootstrap_ap_ci(classified, total_positives, config) -> (f64, f64)
    // 1. Separate TP and FP items
    // 2. Stratified resample: resample TP and FP independently to preserve class ratio
    // 3. Recompute AP per sample
    // 4. Sort AP samples, report percentiles at alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2

Add to EvalMetrics:

    pub ap_ci_lower: Option<f64>,
    pub ap_ci_upper: Option<f64>,

**Integration with regression (scratch-md2t):** If baseline AP falls within current CI, verdict = PASS even if point estimate dropped. Prevents false-alarm regressions from sampling noise.

**Tests:**
- Perfect classifier: CI = (1.0, 1.0)
- Proptest: ci_lower <= AP <= ci_upper
- Determinism: same seed -> same CI
- rand crate already in workspace (check Cargo.lock)

### C. F2 Score (Recall-Weighted)

**Research basis:**
- Neptune.ai, sklearn F-beta docs [evidence 3]
- F1 weights P and R equally. For secret scanning, FN (missed secret) is costlier than FP (false alert). F2 weights recall 4x more: F2 = 5*P*R / (4*P + R)

**Implementation — 3 lines:**

    let f2 = safe_div(5.0 * precision * recall, 4.0 * precision + recall);

Add to EvalMetrics: pub f2: f64

**Test:** Perfect classifier: f2 == 1.0. All FP: f2 == 0.0.

### D. Confirmed: Do NOT add ROC-AUC

- Davis & Goadrich ICML 2006, Saito & Rehmsmeier PLOS ONE 2015, Coralogix guide all confirm ROC-AUC is wrong for imbalanced detection.
- Negatives dominate by orders of magnitude in secret scanning.
- Our step-function AP with tie-collapsing matches sklearn post-v0.19. No change needed.

### References
1. Davis & Goadrich, ICML 2006 — PR vs ROC curves
2. Saito & Rehmsmeier, PLOS ONE 2015 — PR-AUC computation, bootstrap CIs
3. sklearn average_precision_score docs — reference implementation
4. Coralogix PR-AUC guide — https://coralogix.com/ai-blog/ultimate-guide-to-pr-auc-calculations-uses-and-limitations/
5. Neptune.ai — precision/recall at fixed thresholds
6. Chicco & Jurman, BMC Genomics 2020 — MCC vs F1 (contrarian, not adopted)
